title: Webflow to Close CRM Webhook Setup Guide
content:
How to Sync Webflow with Close CRM via Webhooks#This guide details the process of synchronizing data from Webflow to Close CRM using raw webhooks, bypassing third-party integration platforms for direct, custom control. As a principal integration engineer, this approach offers maximum flexibility and performance.
1. Prerequisites (Authentication, Keys, API requirements)#Successful integration necessitates specific access and understanding of both platforms’ capabilities and authentication mechanisms.
Webflow:
Webflow Site Access: Administrative access to your Webflow project settings. Form/CMS Structure: A clear understanding of the data fields within your Webflow Forms or the structure of your CMS Collections that will trigger the synchronization. No API Key for Outgoing Webhooks: Webflow does not require an API key to send webhooks. Its internal system authorizes outbound calls from your project. Close CRM:
Close CRM API Key: A personal API key generated within your Close CRM account. This key is crucial for authenticating all API requests. Location: Navigate to Settings > API Keys within Close CRM. Generate a new key if one doesn’t exist or retrieve an existing one. Usage: The API key is used for HTTP Basic Authentication. It should be used as the username, with an empty string as the password. Close CRM API Endpoint: All API interactions occur via https://api.close.com/api/v1/. Specific resources (e.g., lead/, contact/) append to this base URL. Data Models: Familiarity with Close CRM’s data models (e.g., Leads, Contacts, Opportunities) is essential for correctly mapping Webflow data. This guide will primarily focus on creating Leads. API Rate Limits: Be aware of Close CRM’s API rate limits (e.g., 200 requests per minute per API key) to ensure your integration scales appropriately without hitting throttling thresholds. Implement robust error handling and potentially rate limiting in your webhook receiver if high volumes are expected. Integration Middleware (Webhook Receiver):
Server-Side Component: A critical component for this integration is a custom server-side application (e.g., Node.js script, Python Flask app, AWS Lambda function, Google Cloud Function) that will: Receive the incoming POST requests from Webflow webhooks. Parse the JSON payload from Webflow. Transform the Webflow data into a format suitable for the Close CRM API. Authenticate with Close CRM using your API key. Make the necessary API call(s) to Close CRM. Handle responses and log any errors. Publicly Accessible URL: This middleware must be hosted on a publicly accessible URL for Webflow to send webhooks to it. 2. Setting up the Trigger in Webflow#This section outlines how to configure Webflow to send a webhook when a specific event occurs, such as a form submission.
Navigate to Project Settings: In your Webflow Designer, click the “W” icon in the top left, then select Project Settings. Access Integrations: Go to the Integrations tab. Locate Webhooks: Scroll down to the Webhooks section. Add New Webhook: Click the + Add new webhook button. Configure Webhook Details: Trigger Type: Select the event that will initiate the webhook. Common triggers include: Form submission: Ideal for capturing lead generation forms. Collection item created: For syncing new CMS entries (e.g., blog posts, product listings) as leads or opportunities. Collection item updated: For syncing changes to existing CMS entries. Webhook URL: This is the URL of your custom webhook receiver script (the middleware described in Section 1). Ensure this URL is publicly accessible and configured to handle POST requests. Name: Provide a descriptive name for your webhook (e.g., “New Contact Form Submission to Close CRM”). Add Webhook: Click Add webhook to save your configuration. Example Webflow Form Submission Payload: When a form is submitted, Webflow sends a POST request to your specified Webhook URL with a JSON body similar to this:
{ "triggerType": "form_submission", "data": { "_id": "653b61889c3e20e8a7d1e1f1", "name": "Website Contact Form", "siteId": "653b61889c3e20e8a7d1e1f0", "submittedAt": "2023-10-27T14:30:00.000Z", "ipAddress": "203.0.113.45", "fieldData": { "Name": "Jane Doe", "Email": "jane.doe@example.com", "Company": "Acme Solutions", "Phone": "+1 (555) 123-4567", "Message": "I'm interested in learning more about your services. Please contact me." } } }Note: The fieldData object contains the actual form input values, where keys correspond to your Webflow form field names.
3. Webhook Payload & Endpoint Configuration for Close CRM#This section details the critical middleware component responsible for transforming Webflow data and sending it to Close CRM.
Your custom webhook receiver script will perform the following actions:
Receive Webhook: Listen for incoming POST requests at the configured Webflow Webhook URL.
Parse Payload: Extract the JSON body from the incoming request.
Data Extraction & Transformation: Parse the fieldData from the Webflow payload and map it to the corresponding fields in Close CRM’s Lead or Contact object.
For a Webflow form submission (as shown above), you might map fieldData.Name to a Close Contact’s name, fieldData.Email to an email address, fieldData.Company to the Lead’s name, and fieldData.Message to the Lead’s description. Construct Close CRM API Request: Create a JSON payload that conforms to the Close CRM API’s requirements for creating a Lead.
Endpoint: https://api.close.com/api/v1/lead/ HTTP Method: POST Authentication: Authorization: Basic [Base64_Encoded(YOUR_API_KEY:)] Headers: Content-Type: application/json Example Close CRM Lead Creation Payload: Based on the Webflow form data above, the middleware would construct a Close CRM Lead payload like this:
{ "name": "Acme Solutions - Jane Doe Inquiry", // Derived from Webflow Company + Name "description": "I'm interested in learning more about your services. Please contact me. (Submitted via Webflow 'Website Contact Form' on 2023-10-27)", "status_id": "stat_xxxxxxx", // Optional: Use a specific Close CRM status ID for new leads "url": "https://www.acmesolutions.com", // Optional: If your form captures a website URL "contacts": [ { "name": "Jane Doe", "emails": [ { "email": "jane.doe@example.com", "type": "work" } ], "phones": [ { "phone": "+15551234567", "type": "mobile" } ] } ] } Important considerations for the middleware script: Error Handling: Implement robust try-catch blocks. Log all incoming payloads and outgoing API responses for debugging. Validation: Sanitize and validate incoming data from Webflow before sending it to Close CRM to prevent malformed requests. Idempotency: Consider implementing idempotency keys (if Close CRM supports them) to prevent duplicate lead creation if a webhook is retried. Security: Ensure your webhook receiver is secured, perhaps by validating a Webflow signature header (if provided, though not standard for simple form submissions) or by restricting access to known IPs. 4. Testing and Validating the Data Sync#Thorough testing is crucial to ensure data flows correctly and reliably.
Deploy Middleware: Ensure your custom webhook receiver script is deployed to its public URL and is actively listening for POST requests. Verify it’s accessible (e.g., using curl -X POST -d '{}' YOUR_WEBHOOK_URL).
Configure Webflow Webhook: Double-check that the “Webhook URL” in your Webflow Project Settings exactly matches the URL of your deployed middleware.
Trigger Test Event:
Form Submission: Go to your live Webflow site and submit the form that is configured to trigger the webhook. Use realistic test data. CMS Item: If your webhook is for a CMS item, create or update a test item in the Webflow CMS. Monitor Webflow Webhook Logs:
In Webflow Project Settings > Integrations > Webhooks, find your webhook. Click View Logs to see if Webflow successfully delivered the webhook payload to your middleware. Look for 200 OK responses, indicating successful delivery to your endpoint. 4xx or 5xx responses indicate an issue with your middleware or its accessibility. Monitor Middleware Logs:
Access the logs for your custom webhook receiver. Verify that it received the Webflow payload, processed it, and made an API call to Close CRM. Look for any errors during parsing, data transformation, or the API call to Close CRM. Ensure the Close CRM API call returned a 200 OK or 201 Created status code. Verify in Close CRM:
Log into your Close CRM account. Navigate to the Leads section. Search for the lead or contact that should have been created or updated. Crucially, verify the data accuracy: Is the lead name correct? Are the contact details (name, email, phone) accurate? Is the description populated as expected? Are any custom fields correctly mapped (if you extended the example)? Is the lead status set correctly? Edge Case Testing (Optional but Recommended):
Missing Fields: Test what happens if required fields in your Webflow form are left blank. Does your middleware handle this gracefully, or does it throw an error? Invalid Data: Submit an email in an incorrect format. Ensure Close CRM or your middleware rejects it or logs an error. Duplicate Submissions: While not always required for simple form submissions, consider how your system would handle rapid, identical submissions. By meticulously following these steps, you can establish a robust, direct data synchronization pipeline between Webflow and Close CRM using raw webhooks.

title: Webflow to Linear Webhook Setup Guide
content:
This guide outlines the technical process for synchronizing data from Webflow to Linear using raw Webhooks, focusing on a robust, custom integration approach. As a Principal Integration Engineer, I emphasize precision in payload handling and API interaction.
How to Sync Webflow with Linear via Webhooks#1. Prerequisites (Authentication, Keys, API requirements)#Before initiating data synchronization, ensure the following foundational elements are in place. This setup requires an intermediary service (e.g., a serverless function like AWS Lambda, Google Cloud Functions, or a custom application) to receive Webflow webhooks and interface with the Linear GraphQL API.
Webflow Account:
Admin Access: Required to configure Webhooks within your project settings. CMS Collection: The target Collection containing the data you intend to synchronize (e.g., “Blog Posts,” “Feature Requests”). Ensure CMS items have relevant fields (e.g., Name, Slug, Description) that will map to Linear issue properties. Linear Account:
API Key: Generate a personal API key from your Linear settings (Settings > API > Personal API Keys). This key provides authenticated access to your Linear workspace and teams. Treat this key as sensitive information. Team ID: You will need the ID of the Linear team where issues will be created. This can be found by inspecting the URL of a team page in Linear (https://app.linear.app/team/<TEAM_ID>) or via the Linear GraphQL API. Project ID (Optional): If you intend to associate issues with specific projects, obtain the relevant Project ID similarly. Workflow State IDs (Optional): To create issues in a specific workflow state (e.g., “Backlog,” “Triage”), you’ll need the corresponding state IDs. Integration Layer:
Webhook Receiver Endpoint: A publicly accessible HTTP POST endpoint capable of receiving JSON payloads from Webflow. This endpoint will parse the Webflow data and construct appropriate requests for Linear. Programming Language/Runtime: Familiarity with a language capable of making HTTP requests (e.g., Node.js, Python, Go) and parsing JSON. Network Access: The integration layer must be able to make outbound requests to https://api.linear.app/graphql. 2. Setting up the Trigger in Webflow#Webflow Webhooks initiate the data synchronization by sending a POST request to your designated endpoint whenever a specified event occurs within a CMS collection.
Access Webflow Project Settings: Navigate to your Webflow project, then go to Project Settings > Integrations > Webhooks.
Add New Webhook: Click “Add New Webhook”.
Configure Webhook Details:
Trigger Type: Select the event that should trigger the sync. Common choices for synchronizing new content or requests include: CMS item created: For new content/items. CMS item updated: For changes to existing content. Form submission: If you’re syncing form data as Linear issues. For this guide, we’ll primarily focus on CMS item created. Collection: Choose the specific CMS Collection you want to monitor (e.g., “Blog Posts”). Webhook URL: Enter the full URL of your custom integration layer’s receiver endpoint (e.g., https://your-integration-layer.com/webflow-webhook). Auth (Optional but Recommended): While Webflow doesn’t natively support custom headers for webhooks, if your integration layer requires authentication (e.g., an API key in the URL query string or path), configure your endpoint accordingly. For simplicity in this raw webhook guide, we assume the endpoint is secured at the infrastructure level or relies on the inherent difficulty of guessing the URL. Add Webhook: Click “Add Webhook” to save the configuration.
Upon a successful trigger event, Webflow will send a JSON payload to your specified Webhook URL. The structure typically resembles:
{ "triggerType": "cms_item_created", "data": { "collectionId": "6543210fedcba9876543210f", "itemId": "0fedcba9876543210fedcba9", "item": { "_archived": false, "_cid": "6543210fedcba9876543210f", "_draft": false, "_id": "0fedcba9876543210fedcba9", "name": "New Feature Request: User Profile Management", "slug": "new-feature-request-user-profile-management", "created-on": "2023-10-27T10:00:00.000Z", "updated-on": "2023-10-27T10:00:00.000Z", "published-on": "2023-10-27T10:00:00.000Z", "description": "Users need to be able to update their profile information, including name, email, and password.", "status": "Submitted" // ... other custom fields from your CMS item } } }3. Webhook Payload & Endpoint Configuration for Linear#This section details the logic for your custom integration layer, which acts as the bridge between Webflow and Linear.
3.1. Receiving and Parsing the Webflow Payload#Your integration layer’s endpoint must listen for HTTP POST requests and parse the incoming JSON.
// Example (Node.js/Express) app.post('/webflow-webhook', (req, res) => { const webflowPayload = req.body; if (webflowPayload.triggerType === 'cms_item_created') { const itemName = webflowPayload.data.item.name; const itemDescription = webflowPayload.data.item.description || "No description provided."; const webflowItemId = webflowPayload.data.item._id; // Log the payload for debugging console.log('Received Webflow CMS item created:', itemName); // Proceed to create Linear issue createLinearIssue(itemName, itemDescription, webflowItemId) .then(() => res.status(200).send('Linear issue created successfully.')) .catch(error => { console.error('Error creating Linear issue:', error); res.status(500).send('Failed to create Linear issue.'); }); } else { res.status(200).send('Ignored non-creation trigger type.'); } });3.2. Constructing the Linear GraphQL Request#Linear’s API is GraphQL-based, meaning you send a single POST request to https://api.linear.app/graphql with a GraphQL mutation in the request body.
API Endpoint: https://api.linear.app/graphql HTTP Method: POST Headers: Content-Type: application/json Authorization: Bearer <YOUR_LINEAR_API_KEY> Request Body (JSON): Contains query (the GraphQL mutation string) and variables (an object mapping variable names in the query to their values). Example GraphQL Mutation for Creating an Issue:#// Function within your integration layer async function createLinearIssue(title, description, webflowItemId) { const LINEAR_API_KEY = process.env.LINEAR_API_KEY; // Securely load from environment variables const LINEAR_TEAM_ID = "YOUR_LINEAR_TEAM_ID"; // Replace with your actual Team ID const LINEAR_PROJECT_ID = "YOUR_LINEAR_PROJECT_ID"; // Optional: Replace with your actual Project ID // For a specific workflow state, e.g., "Triage" or "Backlog" const LINEAR_STATE_ID = "YOUR_LINEAR_WORKFLOW_STATE_ID"; const graphqlQuery = ` mutation IssueCreate($title: String!, $description: String, $teamId: String!, $projectId: String, $stateId: String) { issueCreate( input: { title: $title, description: $description, teamId: $teamId, projectId: $projectId, stateId: $stateId, # Optionally add Webflow item ID as a custom field or link in description # e.g., 'Webflow Item ID: ${webflowItemId}' or update a custom field if configured } ) { success issue { id title url } lastSyncId } } `; const variables = { title: title, description: `[Webflow CMS] - ${description}\n\nWebflow Item ID: ${webflowItemId}`, teamId: LINEAR_TEAM_ID, projectId: LINEAR_PROJECT_ID, // Include if using projects stateId: LINEAR_STATE_ID // Include if setting initial state }; const requestBody = { query: graphqlQuery, variables: variables }; try { const response = await fetch('https://api.linear.app/graphql', { method: 'POST', headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json', 'Authorization': `Bearer ${LINEAR_API_KEY}` }, body: JSON.stringify(requestBody) }); const data = await response.json(); if (data.errors) { console.error("Linear API errors:", data.errors); throw new Error(data.errors.map(e => e.message).join(", ")); } if (data.data.issueCreate.success) { console.log(`Successfully created Linear issue: ${data.data.issueCreate.issue.title} (URL: ${data.data.issueCreate.issue.url})`); return data.data.issueCreate.issue; } else { throw new Error("Failed to create Linear issue (success: false)."); } } catch (error) { console.error("Error communicating with Linear API:", error); throw error; } }Obtaining Linear IDs (Team, Project, State): To get teamId, projectId, and stateId programmatically, you can perform GraphQL queries against the Linear API using your personal API key. For instance, to get team IDs:
query { teams { nodes { id name } } }Similarly for projects and workflow states within a team.
4. Testing and Validating the Data Sync#Thorough testing is critical to ensure the integration functions as expected.
Manual Trigger in Webflow:
In your Webflow Designer, navigate to the specific CMS Collection you configured. Create a new CMS item with relevant data (e.g., a new “Blog Post” with a title and description). Publish the item (if your webhook is configured for CMS item published) or save/create it (if configured for CMS item created). This action will send the webhook. Monitor Integration Layer Logs:
Immediately after triggering the event in Webflow, check the logs of your custom integration layer. Look for evidence of the Webflow webhook being received, parsed, and the subsequent HTTP request to the Linear API. Verify any console.log or print statements you included for debugging, especially those indicating success or failure in calling the Linear API. Verify Issue Creation in Linear:
Log into your Linear workspace. Navigate to the team or project where the issue should have been created. Confirm that a new issue with the title and description from your Webflow CMS item has appeared. Check for data accuracy: Is the issue title correct? Is the description populated as expected, including any appended Webflow item ID? Is it assigned to the correct team and project (if specified)? Is the workflow state correct? Troubleshooting Common Issues:
Webhook Not Received: Double-check the “Webhook URL” in Webflow for typos or incorrect protocol (HTTP vs. HTTPS). Ensure your integration layer endpoint is publicly accessible and running. Verify the Webflow trigger type matches your action (e.g., cms_item_created vs. cms_item_published). Linear API Key Issues: Ensure the Authorization header is correctly formatted (Bearer <KEY>). Verify the API key is active and has the necessary permissions in Linear. GraphQL Mutation Errors: Linear’s API is strict. Check the data.errors array in the Linear API response for detailed error messages. Common errors include invalid teamId, projectId, stateId, or missing required fields in the input for issueCreate. Validate the graphqlQuery syntax using a GraphQL client or playground. Data Mapping Issues: Inspect the webflowPayload in your logs to confirm the item data structure matches your expectations. Verify that itemName and itemDescription are correctly extracted and passed to the Linear mutation variables. By following these steps, you establish a reliable and automated data flow from Webflow to Linear, streamlining your content and project management workflows.

title: Webflow to Supabase Webhook Setup Guide
content:
How to Sync Webflow with Supabase via Webhooks#As a principal integration engineer, synchronizing data between platforms like Webflow, the “agentic web platform for modern businesses,” and Supabase is a common requirement for high-performing brands. While Webflow excels in visual development and CMS management, often allowing teams and “AI agents into one shared workspace” for design and content, Supabase provides a powerful, open-source backend for data storage, authentication, and real-time capabilities. This guide outlines a highly accurate, raw webhook-based method for keeping your data consistent between these two systems.
1. Prerequisites (Authentication, Keys, API requirements)#Before establishing the synchronization, ensure you have the necessary access and configurations in place for both Webflow and Supabase.
Webflow Requirements:#Webflow Account & Project: Access to an active Webflow account with a project that includes at least one CMS Collection (e.g., Blog Posts, Products, Services). This will be the source of your data. Collection Structure: Familiarity with your Webflow CMS Collection’s field structure is crucial, as this dictates the data you’ll be syncing. Permissions: You must have administrative access to the Webflow project settings to configure webhooks. Supabase Requirements:#Supabase Project: An active Supabase project. You can create one via the Supabase Studio. Database URL & API Keys: Project URL: Found in Supabase Studio -> Project Settings -> API. anon (public) key: While suitable for client-side, for server-side operations within a Supabase Edge Function, the service_role key is preferred for enhanced permissions. service_role key: This key grants full read/write access and should never be exposed client-side. It will be used securely within your Supabase Edge Function. Target Table: A pre-defined table in your Supabase database designed to store the synchronized Webflow data. Schema Example (webflow_items table): CREATE TABLE public.webflow_items ( id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(), webflow_id TEXT UNIQUE NOT NULL, -- Webflow's unique item ID collection_slug TEXT NOT NULL, -- Webflow collection identifier name TEXT, -- Example field: Webflow item name raw_data JSONB, -- Store the entire Webflow payload for flexibility updated_at TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE DEFAULT timezone('utc'::text, now()) NOT NULL ); ALTER TABLE public.webflow_items ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY; Supabase Edge Functions CLI: For developing and deploying Edge Functions locally before pushing to production. (supabase functions deploy) Basic API Knowledge: Understanding of HTTP methods (POST) and JSON data structures. 2. Setting up the Trigger in Webflow#Webflow’s intuitive interface makes setting up webhook triggers straightforward, leveraging its “no-code” capabilities for integration.
Navigate to Project Settings: In your Webflow Designer, click on the W icon in the top-left corner, then select Project Settings. Access Integrations: Go to the Integrations tab. Webhooks Section: Scroll down to the Webhooks section and click + Add New Webhook. Configure the Webhook: Webhook Name: Provide a descriptive name (e.g., Supabase CMS Sync). Trigger Type: Select the event that should initiate the webhook. Common choices include: CMS item created CMS item updated CMS item deleted You can set up multiple webhooks for different trigger types if needed. Collection: Choose the specific CMS Collection you want to monitor (e.g., Blog Posts, Products). Webhook URL: This is the most critical part. This URL will be the public endpoint of your Supabase Edge Function (or other custom API endpoint) that will receive the Webflow payload. You will obtain this URL after deploying your Edge Function in Supabase. Placeholder URL Example: https://<your-project-ref>.supabase.co/functions/v1/webflow-sync Add Webhook: Click Add Webhook to save your configuration. When the specified event occurs in Webflow (e.g., a new CMS item is created), Webflow will send an HTTP POST request containing a JSON payload to the Webhook URL you provided.
3. Webhook Payload & Endpoint Configuration for Supabase#The core of the synchronization lies in how Supabase receives and processes the Webflow webhook payload. We will use a Supabase Edge Function for this, as it provides a secure, scalable, and integrated environment to handle incoming requests and interact with your database.
Webflow Webhook Payload Example:#Webflow sends a detailed JSON object. A typical payload for cms_item_created or cms_item_updated might look like this:
{ "triggerType": "cms_item_created", "data": { "item": { "_id": "65b9e0728c3d0b2e8a1a3b5c", "name": "My New Product Launch", "slug": "my-new-product-launch", "description": "An exciting new product.", "price": 99.99, "_cid": "65b9e0728c3d0b2e8a1a3b5d", "updatedOn": "2024-03-10T10:00:00.000Z", "createdOn": "2024-03-10T09:00:00.000Z", "publishedOn": "2024-03-10T10:00:00.000Z", "isArchived": false, "isDraft": false, "itemUrl": "https://yourdomain.webflow.io/products/my-new-product-launch" }, "collection": { "_id": "65b9e0728c3d0b2e8a1a3b5d", "name": "Products", "slug": "products" }, "site": { "_id": "65b9e0728c3d0b2e8a1a3b5e", "name": "My Webflow Store", "timezone": "America/New_York" } } }Note: Fields like description, price are custom fields you might have defined in your Webflow CMS collection.
Supabase Edge Function Configuration:#Create an Edge Function: Use the Supabase CLI to create a new function:
supabase functions new webflow-syncThis creates supabase/functions/webflow-sync/index.ts.
Edge Function Code (supabase/functions/webflow-sync/index.ts):
import { createClient } from 'npm:@supabase/supabase-js@2'; import { serve } from 'std/server'; // Initialize Supabase client using environment variables for security const SUPABASE_URL = Deno.env.get('SUPABASE_URL'); const SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY = Deno.env.get('SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY'); if (!SUPABASE_URL || !SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY) { console.error('Missing SUPABASE_URL or SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY environment variables.'); Deno.exit(1); // Exit if keys are not set } const supabase = createClient(SUPABASE_URL, SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY, { auth: { persistSession: false }, // No session persistence needed for server-side }); console.log('Edge Function starting...'); serve(async (req) => { // Ensure the request is a POST request if (req.method !== 'POST') { return new Response(JSON.stringify({ message: 'Method Not Allowed' }), { status: 405, headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }, }); } try { const payload = await req.json(); const { triggerType, data } = payload; if (!data || !data.item || !data.collection) { console.error('Invalid Webflow payload received:', payload); return new Response(JSON.stringify({ message: 'Invalid Webflow payload structure' }), { status: 400, headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }, }); } const webflowItemId = data.item._id; const collectionSlug = data.collection.slug; const itemName = data.item.name; // Extract any other custom fields you need const itemDescription = data.item.description; const itemPrice = data.item.price; console.log(`Processing Webflow item ${webflowItemId} from collection ${collectionSlug} with trigger ${triggerType}`); // Perform upsert operation to insert new items or update existing ones const { data: upsertData, error } = await supabase .from('webflow_items') .upsert( { webflow_id: webflowItemId, collection_slug: collectionSlug, name: itemName, description: itemDescription, // Map custom fields price: itemPrice, // Map custom fields raw_data: payload, // Store the full payload updated_at: new Date().toISOString(), }, { onConflict: 'webflow_id' } // If webflow_id exists, update; otherwise, insert ) .select(); // Select the inserted/updated row if (error) { console.error('Supabase upsert error:', error); return new Response(JSON.stringify({ message: 'Database operation failed', error: error.message }), { status: 500, headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }, }); } console.log('Successfully synced Webflow item:', upsertData); return new Response(JSON.stringify({ message: 'Webhook received and processed', data: upsertData }), { status: 200, headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }, }); } catch (error: any) { console.error('Webhook processing error:', error); return new Response(JSON.stringify({ message: 'Error processing webhook', error: error.message }), { status: 500, headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }, }); } }); Deploy the Edge Function:
supabase functions deploy webflow-sync --no-verify-jwtThe --no-verify-jwt flag is important as Webflow webhooks do not send a JWT, making your Edge Function publicly accessible by URL. For production, consider implementing additional security measures like IP whitelisting or a custom shared secret header validation (which Webflow doesn’t natively support, requiring an intermediary).
After deployment, Supabase CLI will provide the public URL for your Edge Function. Copy this URL and paste it into the Webflow Webhook URL field (from Section 2).
4. Testing and Validating the Data Sync#Thorough testing is crucial to ensure your data synchronization pipeline is robust.
Trigger the Webhook from Webflow:
In your Webflow Designer, navigate to the CMS Collection you configured (e.g., Products). Create: Add a new item to the collection and publish it. Update: Modify an existing item and publish the changes. Delete (if configured): Delete an item. Each action should trigger the respective webhook. Monitor Webhook Delivery in Webflow:
Return to Project Settings > Integrations > Webhooks in Webflow. Look at the “Webhook Logs” section. You should see entries for your Supabase CMS Sync webhook. A successful delivery will show an HTTP 2xx status code. If you see errors, click on the log entry for more details. Validate Data in Supabase:
In your Supabase Studio, navigate to the Table Editor and select your webflow_items table. Verify that new rows appear for created items and existing rows are updated for modified items. Check the raw_data JSONB column to ensure the full payload was stored correctly. You can also use the SQL Editor to query your table: SELECT * FROM public.webflow_items ORDER BY updated_at DESC; Monitor Supabase Edge Function Logs:
In Supabase Studio, go to Edge Functions and select your webflow-sync function. Check the Logs tab. You should see the console.log messages from your function, indicating successful processing or any errors encountered during execution. Troubleshooting Common Issues:#Webflow Webhook Delivery Failure (HTTP 4xx/5xx): Incorrect Webhook URL: Double-check that the URL entered in Webflow precisely matches your deployed Supabase Edge Function URL. Supabase Edge Function Not Deployed/Active: Ensure your function is deployed and running. Network Issues: Temporarily unreachable endpoint. Supabase Edge Function Errors (Internal Server Error - 500): Environment Variables: Verify that SUPABASE_URL and SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY are correctly set as environment variables for your Edge Function in Supabase Studio. Code Bugs: Review your Edge Function code for syntax errors, incorrect table names, or logical flaws. Use the function logs for detailed error messages. Database Schema Mismatch: Ensure the column names and data types in your webflow_items table match what your Edge Function is trying to upsert. No Data in Supabase (but Webhook shows success): The Edge Function might be running but failing silently after receiving the payload, perhaps due to an issue with the supabase client or the upsert operation not being handled correctly. Check the Edge Function logs thoroughly. Row Level Security (RLS) policies on your webflow_items table might be blocking the service_role key (though less likely if service_role is used and RLS allows insert and update for service_role). By following these steps, you can establish a robust, real-time data synchronization between Webflow and Supabase, empowering your “agentic web platform” with a powerful backend for enhanced functionality.
